page_hint: Ch 17 §4 (Measurement, 'Which one drives KV residency?') vs §8 (Mini-Case, 'Initial sizing analysis' and 'Decision')
quoted_clause: §4: "Do not substitute a p95/p99 for E[W] in Little's Law. Little's Law is a *mean* relation, E[L] = λ·E[W]; pairing a mean λ with a p95 W mixes moments and yields a number that is neither a mean population nor a percentile one."  §8: "At T = 3 (the 95th-percentile, and the honest stress-cohort sizing point — 'worst case' applies only to the 2% fallback route, F-01) ... N ≈ ⌈1,770/(13 × 0.70 × 0.95)⌉ = ⌈1,770/8.645⌉ ≈ **205 working hosts**" and "the integer-slot FP8 bound under **no-reuse** is **99 working hosts at the 70% × 95% policy, plus one spare host for N−1 operation: 100 hosts in total**"
observed: The chapter states a hard rule (percentile W must not be substituted into the mean Little's Law identity) and then bases its entire mini-case decision on the 95th-percentile turn count T=3, with no mean-based fleet count anywhere in the chapter. The chapter's own F-01 box supplies the distribution-weighted mean W ≈ 12.71 s but never converts it into a host count, so the reader is left with a single (stress-cohort) number presented as 'the Decision'.
evidence: Recomputation from the chapter's own inputs: distribution 0.68/0.25/0.05/0.02 over T=1/2/3/fallback; I(1)=10,365, I(2)=11,230, I(3)=12,095, I(fallback)=9,500 tokens; κ=2.62144 MB/token → per-request KV 27.171 / 29.438 / 31.705 / 24.904 GB; distribution-weighted mean bytes ≈ 0.68(27.171)+0.25(29.438)+0.05(31.705)+0.02(24.904) ≈ 27.92 GB → C = 436/27.92 ≈ 15.6 → floor 15. With F-01's mean W ≈ 12.71 s at 100 rps: in-flight ≈ 1,271 → N = ⌈1,271/(15×0.70×0.95)⌉ = ⌈1,271/9.975⌉ = ⌈127.4⌉ ≈ 128 working hosts (FP16) — versus the 205 the chapter reports for the same traffic point. The stress-cohort figure is ~1.6× the mean-based figure. (The mean-based number is itself approximate because E[bytes×time] ≠ E[bytes]·E[time], which the chapter itself notes.)
root_cause: The chapter separates 'mean' and 'stress cohort' ledgers in F-01 but never propagates the mean ledger into the sizing output; the mini-case's decision line inherits the stress cohort without qualification.
correction: Add the distribution-weighted mean case as a first-class row of Table 17-2 (or a second mini-case column): mean W ≈ 12.71 s, mean per-request KV ≈ 27.9 GB, C ≈ 15 (floor), and the resulting N at 40/100/200 rps. Then state explicitly which number is the planning decision (e.g. 'size to the mean, hold the stress cohort as the tail-risk bound') and label the T=3 columns as the stress bound they are. Reconcile the §4 rule with the §8 practice by pointing at the new mean row rather than at F-01's caveat.
acceptance_test: Table 17-2 contains a distribution-weighted-mean row whose N values are reproducible from F-01's mean W and the distribution-weighted mean bytes; the mini-case's 'Decision' paragraph names which row is the decision and which is the bound; no sentence in Ch 17 pairs a percentile W with a mean Little's Law identity without an explicit stress-cohort label.

page_hint: Ch 17 §4 ('The KV population is its own derivation' paragraph)
quoted_clause: "then adjusted for the **rank/replication layout** (tensor-parallel rank count, and whether KV is sharded across ranks or replicated) and the **admission policy** (whole-context admission with no fractional slots; a prefix-cache hit or a pre-reserved block changes the effective holding time, not the byte geometry)."
observed: The claim that a prefix-cache hit changes 'the effective holding time, not the byte geometry' is incorrect for the mechanism the chapter elsewhere relies on. When a prefix is shared across requests, the marginal KV bytes attributable to a new request are the *delta* (the newly appended tokens), not the whole context; the cached prefix is resident once and reused. The chapter's own reuse scenario (§8, W=14.16 s) is built on exactly this mechanism, so the statement contradicts the chapter's use of prefix caching.
evidence: In §8's reuse case the prefill of the final call is 11,795 tokens of which 9,200 are the cached prefix; the KV for those 9,200 tokens is resident once per shared prefix, not once per request. The chapter nevertheless keeps C = 13 (full 12,095-token context) for the reuse rows of Table 17-2, i.e. it charges every request for the whole context while simultaneously claiming the prefix is shared. The two statements cannot both be true; the reuse rows are conservative in bytes but the accompanying mechanism claim is wrong.
root_cause: The 'byte geometry' sentence was written to prevent a specific transplant error (queue time into KV slots) and over-generalized into a claim about prefix caching, which is a different mechanism.
correction: Split the sentence: (a) a pre-reserved block changes the *holding time* (and can change the admission granularity), not the per-request byte geometry; (b) a prefix-cache hit changes *both* — the marginal bytes per request (delta-only) and the effective holding time — and its capacity benefit depends on the prefix-hit rate and on whether the cached prefix is shared across concurrent requests or pinned to one. Then state which assumption the reuse rows of Table 17-2 use (full-context C, i.e. no byte credit for prefix sharing) and label it as conservative.
acceptance_test: The chapter contains no sentence asserting that prefix caching leaves byte geometry unchanged; Table 17-2's reuse rows state explicitly whether any byte credit is taken for shared prefixes, and the §8 reuse narrative is consistent with that statement.

quoted_clause: "Under case (i) the available headroom is only ~7%; under cases (ii) and (iii) the prefill leg alone exceeds the idealized ceiling, so headroom is negative — the real headroom is smaller than ~7% and may be negative."  vs  "the check pushes the real count upward — by at least the ~7% headroom deficit under case (i), and by more than that under cases (ii)/(iii), where the prefill leg already exceeds the ceiling."
observed: The same 7% is described as 'available headroom' in one sentence and as a 'headroom deficit' in the next. Under case (i) the prefill leg consumes 93% of the ceiling, so the deficit is negative (there is 7% of headroom, not a 7% shortfall). The second sentence then uses the deficit to claim the host count must be pushed upward by 'at least ~7%', which does not follow from a positive 7% headroom.
evidence: 18,400 ÷ 19,780 = 0.9302 → headroom 6.98%. A 7% headroom means the prefill leg could grow by 7% before the ceiling binds; it does not imply a 7% capacity shortfall. The upward push under case (i) is already captured by the policy screens reported elsewhere in the chapter (⌈18.60/0.665⌉+1 = 29 for case (i), versus 32 for the KV-only policy total), so the paragraph double-counts the effect it claims to add.
root_cause: The paragraph was written as a 'the check pushes the count up' narrative and reuses the 7% figure with the wrong sign, without reconciling against the policy-level prefill screens already tabulated in Table 17-1's caption and Table 17-2's note.
correction: Rewrite the paragraph to state the sign correctly: under case (i) the prefill leg leaves ~7% headroom at full utilization, so the prefill screen (18.60 hosts) does not bind against the KV screen (21 hosts); under cases (ii)/(iii) it binds. Then point to the already-reported policy-level screens (29 / 32 / 34) as the place where the prefill constraint enters the host count, instead of asserting an additional upward push.
acceptance_test: The word 'deficit' is not applied to the case-(i) 7% figure anywhere in Ch 17; the 'Effect on the headline counts' paragraph cites the same 29/32/34 policy screens as Table 17-1 and Table 17-2 rather than introducing a separate, unsourced increment.

quoted_clause: "Alerts should trigger when per-host concurrency exceeds 80% of C, when LB error rate exceeds 0.1%, or when cross-host bandwidth utilization exceeds 70%."
observed: The concurrency alert threshold (80% of C) is looser than the chapter's own operating-utilization ceiling u = 0.70 (Table 17-1). The fleet is provisioned so that per-host concurrency stays at or below 70% of C; an alert that fires only at 80% of C therefore fires after the fleet has already violated its own sizing policy, and never fires in the regime the policy is designed to prevent.
evidence: Table 17-1: u = 0.70, 'max operating-utilization target', '**independent** of ρ — multiplies the denominator'. §4: 'The provisioning formula's effective slot count is C × u × ρ = 13 × 0.70 × 0.95 = 8.645'. With N = ⌈708/8.645⌉ = 82 hosts at 40 rps, planned occupancy is 708/(82×13) = 66.4% of C — i.e. the fleet is deliberately run at ~66%, below the 70% ceiling and far below the 80% alert.
root_cause: The observability thresholds were written as generic operational defaults rather than being derived from the chapter's own provisioning policy.
correction: Derive the alert thresholds from the policy: page at 70% of C (the u ceiling) and treat 80% of C as a hard capacity-exhaustion threshold, or state explicitly that the 80% figure is a separate 'capacity exhausted' alarm and add a 70% 'policy breach' warning. Also state the metric definition (resident sequences vs admitted requests) so the alert is measurable.
acceptance_test: Every numeric threshold in §6 is either derived from Table 17-1's u/ρ policy or explicitly labelled as an independent operational default with a rationale; no alert threshold is looser than the utilization ceiling the chapter sizes to without explanation.

quoted_clause: §8: "The proposed design uses NGINX with consistent hashing for session affinity and OpenTelemetry tracing on each host."  §6: "(b) if stateless, use least-connections or power-of-two-choices so load follows capacity — do not use consistent hashing."
observed: The mini-case's design decision selects consistent hashing for session affinity, which the chapter explicitly forbids for stateless routing. The canonical workload is stateless: §3 states 'In the canonical scenario, requests are independent — no user session spans multiple hosts', and §2 states that stateless routing gives even distribution. The decision therefore adopts the option the chapter rules out, without stating a session-affinity requirement that would justify it.
evidence: §3: 'Cross-host communication. In the canonical scenario, requests are independent — no user session spans multiple hosts.' §2: 'If sessions are stateless ... any host can serve any request, and load distribution becomes even.' §6: 'do not use consistent hashing' for the stateless case.
root_cause: The mini-case's decision line appears to have been written from a generic 'production design' template rather than from the chapter's own routing rule; the session-affinity requirement is never established for the scenario.
correction: Either (a) change the decision to least-connections / power-of-two-choices and state that the canonical workload is stateless, or (b) establish in the scenario that sessions must be sticky (e.g. multi-turn conversations with retained KV), and then justify consistent hashing against the §2 density-vs-evenness trade-off and the §5 mistake #2 skew analysis. If (b), the fleet sizing must also account for the reduced effective parallelism that affinity implies.
acceptance_test: The mini-case's LB choice is consistent with §6's routing rule given an explicitly stated session model; if affinity is chosen, the chapter states the affinity requirement and its capacity consequence.

quoted_clause: 'Viability at peak': "Peak traffic is 40 rps; with the canonical ~8.6 s per-request service time ... Little's Law puts ≈ 40 × 8.6 ≈ **344 requests in flight**, against a KV capacity of ~17.5 per host (conservative integer floor 17). **A single host is not viable at peak even for the non-agentic canonical workload** — the fleet needs roughly ⌈344/17⌉ = **21 hosts** at 40 rps (**31 working hosts** at the 70% × 95% provisioning policy, **32 total with N−1** — Table 17-1)"  'Scaling forecast (service-time-aware)': "the in-flight concurrency at the 40 rps peak ... is λ_peak × W ≈ 40 × 8.6 ≈ **344 requests**, not 40. The second adds no new computation, no new assumption, and no new consequence; it re-states the first with a 'not 40' emphasis. quoted_clause: "These are the honest arithmetic bounds the full service-time model produces — the naive '1–5 hosts' rps estimate — never tied to a traffic level — is off by ~16–205× (82 hosts ÷ 5 ≈ 16.4 at the 40-rps peak; 205 ÷ 1 = 205 at the 100-rps peak; each ratio is per its own traffic point)"

The parenthetical's 'each ratio is per its own traffic point' does not repair this: the denominator is the thing that changes, not the traffic point. As written, the comparison is not reproducible and reads as a rhetorical amplification of the chapter's own result.

If a range is retained, use one denominator per traffic point derived from the same naive rule.

page_hint: Ch 17 §8 (Mini-Case, 'Initial sizing analysis') vs Ch 19 references
quoted_clause: "The tool leg here uses the ~133 ms/turn tool/retrieval rate; Chapter 19's `T·L_agent` (~660 ms at T=3) is the *orchestration-only* incremental overhead at a different per-turn rate, and a single model should use one rate consistently."
observed: The chapter acknowledges that two different per-turn tool/orchestration rates are in play (0.133 s/turn here vs 0.22 s/turn implied by Ch 19's T·L_agent ≈ 660 ms at T=3) and states that 'a single model should use one rate consistently' — i.e. it identifies a defect in the book's own model and leaves it in place. The two rates differ by ~65%, and the tool term is ~2% of W(3) = 17.70 s, so the numerical impact on the fleet counts is small; the impact on the book's coherence is not: the same agentic scenario is costed with two different orchestration rates in two chapters.

The chapter's own W(3) = 17.70 s is built on the 133 ms rate; substituting 220 ms/turn gives W(3) ≈ 18.03 s, in-flight 1,803 at 100 rps, N = ⌈1,803/8.645⌉ = 209 (vs 205) — a ~2% change, confirming the numerical stakes are low but the modelling inconsistency is real.
root_cause: Ch 17's evaluator script and Ch 19's β(T) model were parameterised independently; the discrepancy was documented rather than reconciled.
correction: Reconcile in one place: state the canonical per-turn tool/retrieval rate (and whether it includes orchestration), and have both Ch 17's evaluator and Ch 19's β(T) reference it. If the two quantities are genuinely different (retrieval service time vs orchestration overhead), say so explicitly and state which one enters W_KV-resident and which enters W_e2e, then show the effect on W(3) (≈ +0.33 s, ≈ +2% on the host count).
acceptance_test: A single per-turn tool/retrieval rate is used wherever an agentic service time is computed in Ch 17 and Ch 19, or the two rates are explicitly distinguished with their separate roles and their numeric effect on W stated.

page_hint: Ch 17 §2 (Mental Model) vs §4 ('Request traffic and model collectives are different populations')
quoted_clause: §2: "Each backend host runs an identical copy of the model and serves requests independently."  §4: "A distributed model introduces different events. Tensor-parallel participants exchange partial results at layer boundaries; expert-parallel participants dispatch and combine routed tokens."
observed: The chapter's mental model — the frame through which the reader is meant to understand everything that follows — assumes a fleet of independent, identical model replicas. The chapter then introduces collectives (TP/EP) that only exist when a single model spans multiple hosts, without reconciling that topology with the mental model. The reader is never told which fleet topology the canonical 21/31/32 counts assume (replica-per-host) or how a TP-spanning-host fleet would change the sizing arithmetic (the KV screen, the per-host C, and the load-balancer model all change).
evidence: §2's two invariants (throughput ≈ N × per-host; memory = N × per-host) hold only for the replica-per-host topology. §4's collective paragraph explicitly notes that collectives 'follow the actual TP or EP communication group and execution schedule, not the total number of serving hosts', which is incompatible with the §2 frame unless the topology is fixed. The canonical host is 8×H100, so TP=8 is already inside the host; the chapter never states whether the fleet's TP group is confined to a host.
root_cause: The mental model was written for the simple replica fleet and the collectives paragraph was added later as a caveat, without extending the model.
correction: State the topology assumption explicitly in §2 ('the canonical fleet is replica-per-host: each 8×H100 host holds one complete TP=8 model; no TP group crosses a host boundary') and add one sentence in §4 explaining what changes if a TP group does cross hosts (the per-host C and the load-balancer's role change; the KV screen becomes a per-group screen; collectives enter the critical path). This also gives the reader the transfer rule for a future disaggregated-serving topology.
acceptance_test: The fleet topology (replica-per-host vs model-spanning) is stated once in §2 and referenced wherever host counts are derived; §4's collective paragraph opens by naming the topology it applies to.

quoted_clause: "In the worked example, the fleet is currently sized by KV capacity (§17.3), not by a fabricated tokens/s number: at T = 3 (the 95th-percentile sizing point, per the chapter's own rule), FP16-KV C ≈ 13.8/host (436 GB ÷ (12,095 × 2.62 MB ≈ 31.7 GB) ≈ 13.8; conservative integer floor 13) sets the continuous ceiling."
observed: The §4 LB subsection silently switches the sizing point from T=0 (the canonical non-agentic case used for the 21/31/32 headline counts in §3) to T=3, and calls T=3 'the chapter's own rule'. page_hint: Ch 17 §4 (sensitivity band in the 'At the canonical peak' bullet)

acceptance_test: No row of §18.3.2 is described as feasible in a configuration that §18.3.1 computes as infeasible, and every rate used in §18.3.3 is quoted on the basis the table states.

quoted_clause: Under dedicated placement each tier gets its own group: 8-bit C = ⌊506/24.89⌋ = 20 → 13 + 4 + 3 = **20 hosts / 32 with policy**.

quoted_clause: A chat UI tolerates ~200 ms of added service latency per request ... Acceptable for interactive chat (typical threshold: ≤500 ms). ... **Consolidate** when: workload profile overlap ≥70%, latency tolerance ≥300 ms, and cost differential >30%. ... the latency criterion is met against the ≤500 ms interactive threshold of §18.3.4, not the ~200 ms chat tolerance quoted in §18.2 — L̄ ≈ 247 ms clears 500 ms and exceeds 200 ms
observed: The chapter carries two different interactive-chat latency budgets (200 ms in §18.2, 500 ms in §18.3.4) and the consolidation verdict depends on which one applies. Worse, the consolidation criterion is written in terms of the workload's *tolerance* ("latency tolerance ≥300 ms") but is checked against the *achieved* weighted latency (L̄ ≈ 247 ms). Under the criterion as written, the scenario's tolerance is either 200 ms (fails) or 500 ms (passes); under the check as performed, 247 ms fails a 300 ms criterion. The referent note therefore does not actually establish that the criterion is met.
evidence: L̄ = 0.70×250 + 0.20×300 + 0.10×120 = 247 ms (§18.3.4). 247 < 300, so the criterion "latency tolerance ≥300 ms" is not satisfied by the achieved latency under any reading; only the deployment's declared tolerance (500 ms) satisfies it.
root_cause: The criterion was written as a design rule about the workload, then verified with a measurement of the system, and the two were reconciled by prose rather than by rewriting the criterion.
correction: Rewrite the criterion to be about the workload's declared budget, e.g. "latency budget ≥300 ms per request (the deployment's SLO, not the achieved latency)", and state the scenario's budget once, in one place, as 500 ms (the §18.3.4 interactive threshold), removing the 200 ms figure from §18.2 or explicitly marking it as a different quantity (e.g. added service latency above a baseline). Then check the criterion against the declared budget and state the achieved L̄ separately.
acceptance_test: The chapter contains one interactive latency budget, used consistently in §18.2, §18.3.4 and §18.5; the consolidation criterion is stated in terms of the same quantity it is checked against.

quoted_clause: **Scenario:** ~2,000 users, ~5% concurrent (≈100 simultaneous), ~10 rps average / ~40 rps peak. ... For 1,000 requests/hour (≈0.28 rps — a light illustrative load ...)
observed: The chapter's own scenario states ~10 rps average, but the routing arithmetic that produces every headline number in the chapter runs at 1,000 requests/hour = 0.28 rps — 36× below the scenario's average load. The "canonical volume" used for the second savings figure (6.24M requests/month) is ≈2.37 rps average, a third value, and 4.2× below the scenario's 10 rps average (10 rps × 2.628M s/mo ≈ 26.3M requests/month). The scenario's stated load is therefore never used to produce any savings, host count, or cost figure in the chapter, and the peak-to-average ratio implied by the scenario (40/10 = 4×) is inconsistent with the canonical volume paired with the same 40-rps peak (40/2.37 ≈ 17×).
root_cause: Three different traffic bases were introduced at different drafting stages (illustrative 1,000/hr; canonical 6.24M/mo; scenario 10 rps avg / 40 rps peak) and the chapter's caveats explain the bases individually without noticing that they are mutually inconsistent as descriptions of one scenario.
correction: Choose one traffic basis for the chapter's worked example and derive everything from it. If the scenario is 10 rps average / 40 rps peak, state the implied monthly volume (≈26.3M requests/month) and recompute the savings at that volume; if the canonical 6.24M/month is to be used, restate the scenario's average as ≈2.4 rps and reconcile the peak-to-average ratio with Ch 17. Keep the 1,000 req/hr figure only as an explicitly labelled unit-normalization illustration, not as the chapter's savings basis.
acceptance_test: Every rate, volume and savings figure in §18.3 is derived from one stated traffic basis, and the chapter states the peak-to-average ratio it assumes.

quoted_clause: To operate a mixed fleet we measure four cross-cutting metrics:
observed: The table that follows has five rows (weighted average cost/token; per-model throughput; routing accuracy; p95 per-request service latency; token latency p95 per model). The count in the lead-in contradicts the table.
evidence: Table row count = 5.
root_cause: A fifth metric (token latency p95) was added to the table without updating the lead-in.
correction: Change the lead-in to "five cross-cutting metrics", or fold the token-latency diagnostic into the p95 row as a sub-line if it is not intended as a separate metric.
acceptance_test: The stated count equals the number of rows in the table.

quoted_clause: with comparable quality because the 8-bit model is assumed [ASSUMPTION] to meet quality thresholds for ≥90% of requests (no evaluation or benchmark is cited for this figure). ... If a share *q* of the 700 routine requests fails the 8-bit quality bar and escalates to FP16

Read fleet-wide, "≥90% of requests" is inconsistent with the routing split (70% to dense 8-bit, 20% to MoE 8-bit, 10% to FP16 — only 70% of requests are routed to the dense 8-bit tier whose quality bar is at issue). Read within the routine subset, it means q ≤ 10%, which is what the escalation paragraph assumes. The two readings differ by a factor of ~3 in the implied failure population.
evidence: Routing split: 700/200/100 of 1,000 requests. Escalation base: 700 routine requests. 90% of 1,000 = 900 ≠ 700.
root_cause: The assumption was written before the escalation model and never bound to a population.
correction: State the population explicitly: "the 8-bit dense tier is assumed [ASSUMPTION] to meet the quality bar for ≥90% of the requests routed to it (i.e. q ≤ 10% of the 700 routine requests); no evaluation or benchmark is cited." Then note that the 20% MoE share is a routing choice, not a quality failure.
acceptance_test: Every quality assumption in §18.3.3 names the population it applies to, and the escalation base matches it.

page_hint: §18.8 mini-case, Tier 1 memory headroom vs Tier 2

Tier 2 (70B 8-bit dense): ... these ~250-token requests carry ~0.66 GB KV each, so 1×H100's ~10 GB headroom holds ~15 concurrent requests

The Tier 1 figure is therefore not a property of the mini-case's deployment and understates its capacity by more than an order of magnitude.

page_hint: §18.8 mini-case, Tier 1 and the SLO check
quoted_clause: Tier 1 (4-bit GGUF): ... Cost: $0.0002/token, latency ~600 ms. ... **Tier 1 (the cheapest, 4-bit GGUF on CPU, ~600 ms) serves 80% of queries, so the p95 per-request latency is ~600 ms, which violates the 500 ms SLO for the dominant tier.**
observed: The mini-case never states whether its latency figures are TTFT or full-generation time. §18.3.4 establishes that for a CPU 4-bit model the full-generation reading is ~117 s for 250 tokens (~146× the 800 ms ledger figure) and that "only the TTFT reading is defensible". The mini-case's 600 ms is only defensible under the same TTFT reading, but the mini-case applies it as a per-request SLO without saying so, and the SLO verdict (the chapter's central mini-case lesson) therefore rests on an unstated interpretation.

root_cause: The mini-case was written without inheriting the §18.3.4 column-definition note, which is the note that makes the latency numbers meaningful.

quoted_clause: **Ignoring capital amortization.** FP16 on 8×H100 has high upfront cost; spreading that cost across a mixed fleet improves effective cost/token. Don't forget to annualize GPU capex in the per-token math.
observed: The claimed benefit is contradicted by the chapter's own arithmetic: the mixed fleet under the shared placement needs 18–27 more hosts (§18.3.3), so total capital amortization rises, not falls. Spreading a fixed cost over a fleet improves effective cost/token only if the fleet raises utilization of the same capital; the chapter's placement arithmetic shows the opposite. As written, a reader could take away "mixing models lowers capital cost per token" as a general rule.
evidence: §18.3.3: 39 vs 21 hosts (no derate), 58 vs 31 (policy). §18.3.2 basis note: 21 hosts ≈ $155,817/mo.
root_cause: The common-mistakes entry was written as generic advice before the placement arithmetic existed and was never reconciled with it.
correction: Rewrite the correction to the actual mechanism: "amortizing capex over tokens requires utilization, not model diversity. A mixed fleet lowers the token rate only if it raises the utilization of the same installed capital; if it requires additional hosts (as in §18.3.3), total cost per token can rise even as the nominal rate falls."
acceptance_test: No claim in §18.5 asserts a cost benefit that §18.3.3's host arithmetic contradicts.

quoted_clause: N_tail = ⌈λ_tail·W/(C·u·ρ)⌉ = ⌈4 × 8.6/(17 × 0.70 × 0.95)⌉ = ⌈34.4/11.305⌉ ≈ **4 hosts** at the canonical 40-rps peak.

(a) u and ρ are never defined in the chapter, and the same product 0.665 is decomposed differently in §18.3.3, where it is called "the 70%×95% policy" (routing mix × quality pass rate) rather than utilization × ρ. A reader cannot tell whether 0.70 is a utilization factor or the routine-traffic share. (b) The formula uses C = 17, the single-model canonical concurrency, while the chapter's own mixed shared-pool configuration has C = 9 (§18.3.1/§18.3.3); the tail tier (FP16) in the mixed fleet therefore has a different per-host capacity than the formula assumes. The arithmetic itself (34.4/11.305 = 3.04 → 4) is correct.
root_cause: The formula was imported from the single-model chapter (Ch 17) with its symbols intact, and the mixed-fleet configuration was never substituted into it.
correction: Define u and ρ explicitly (e.g. u = target utilization, ρ = policy/quality derate) and use the same decomposition as §18.3.3; state which C applies ("C = 17 for a dedicated FP16 tier; C = 9 for the shared pool of §18.3.3") and give the resulting host count for each.

quoted_clause: | 70B dense FP16 | $2.50 | 120 | capital + energy | ... | 70B 4-bit GGUF | $0.15 | 800 | energy only |
observed: The Basis column mixes two different kinds of content: a cost basis ("capital + energy", "energy only") on two rows and an evidence label ("[ILLUSTRATIVE] example rate, Q4 2026 — not retrieved") on the other two. The two rows carrying a cost basis are also the two rows lacking an evidence label, so the reader cannot tell whether the FP16 and 4-bit rates are measured, derived, or illustrative from the table alone — only from the bases box.

root_cause: The column was overloaded to carry both provenance and basis, and the two label systems were applied to different rows rather than to different columns.
correction: Split into two columns: "Cost basis" (self-amortized capital+energy / public-cloud list / energy-only) and "Evidence" ([ILLUSTRATIVE] / [DERIVED] / [1P]) for every row, so each row carries both.

quoted_clause: 70B dense 8-bit on 2×H100 (or 1×H100 with FP8 KV + offload, shown feasible) — the $1.25/1M rate must be recomputed for that 2×H100 basis before use; 70B MoE 8-bit with 2 active experts; 70B 4-bit GGUF local, no GPU.

The rate in the table ($1.00/1M) therefore has no stated hardware basis at all, which is the same defect as CH18-02 seen from the hardware side.

correction: State the MoE row's hardware explicitly ("70B MoE 8-bit on 2×H100, 2 of 16 experts active") and give every row a hardware + basis pair.
acceptance_test: Every row of the §18.3.2 table names the hardware its rate is quoted on.

quoted_clause: (58 vs 31 — 27 extra hosts; 39 vs 21 — 18 extra — on the no-derate pair)

The intended distinction (the fleet blend is a weighted average across tiers, not a tier's rate) is not made. The target is also trivially met by the chapter's own mixed fleet ($1.33/1M), so it carries no diagnostic value as written.

acceptance_test: The stated target is distinguishable from the tier rate it is compared against, and its provenance is labelled.

quoted_clause: the gate is exercised in §18.3.4, where L̄ = Σ p_i·L_i ≈ 247 ms is checked against the ≤500 ms threshold before the cost ranking is accepted. ... The correct order *within the cost/SLO gate* is: check the SLO, then size the cost
observed: §18.2 asserts that the SLO check precedes acceptance of the cost ranking, but the chapter's own §18.3.3 performs the cost ranking first and §18.3.4 checks the latency afterwards; the mini-case then corrects the order explicitly. The chapter thus states the correct procedure in three places and follows it in none.
evidence: Section order: §18.3.3 routing arithmetic and savings → §18.3.4 latency check → §18.8 "check the SLO before the cost claim".
root_cause: The narrative order of the worked example was fixed before the mini-case's methodological lesson was written, and the lesson was not propagated back.
correction: Either reorder §18.3.3/§18.3.4 so the SLO check precedes the cost ranking, or state in §18.3.3 that the cost ranking is provisional until the §18.3.4 SLO check passes (and note that the 4-bit tier is excluded by the SLO, not by cost).
acceptance_test: The order of operations described in §18.2 matches the order in which §18.3.3 and §18.3.4 present the work.

page_hint: §18.5, Consolidate criteria and the "satisfied by construction" note
quoted_clause: **Consolidate** when: workload profile overlap ≥70%, latency tolerance ≥300 ms, and cost differential >30%. ... *Satisfied by construction in this scenario*: our scenario sits exactly at the threshold — it consolidates 70% of traffic to the dense 8-bit tier — 90% to 8-bit variants once the 20% MoE 8-bit share is counted — at the ≥70% dense-8-bit boundary, not above it
observed: Two of the three criteria have undefined referents. "Workload profile overlap ≥70%" is checked against two different numbers in the same sentence (70% dense-8-bit share, 90% all-8-bit share) and the text concludes the criterion is met "exactly at the threshold" on the 70% reading while the 90% reading would put it above. "Cost differential >30%" does not say between which tiers (8-bit vs FP16 = 50%; 8-bit vs MoE-8-bit = 25%, which would fail). The referent note then asserts the criteria are "satisfied by construction" without resolving either.
root_cause: The criteria were written as generic heuristics and then applied to the scenario without fixing the comparison pairs.
correction: Define each criterion's referent explicitly ("≥70% of requests routed to a single consolidated tier", "cost differential between the consolidated tier and the tier it displaces >30%") and state which pair and which share the scenario satisfies.
acceptance_test: Each consolidation criterion names the quantity it compares, and the scenario's satisfaction of each is checkable from the printed numbers.

The phrase survives in the verdict sentence and is not supported by the chapter's own placement.

quoted_clause: Tier 3 (70B FP16): Handles 5% of queries (complex escalations, multilingual). Runs on 2 GPUs reserved. Cost: $0.003/token, latency ~120 ms.

acceptance_test: All three mini-case tiers state their KV headroom and the request length it is computed against.

acceptance_test: Each quantization claim in §18.5 names the execution device whose behavior it describes.

quoted_clause: the Ch 17 provisioned fleet is 32 hosts, whose amortized rate would be ~$4.01/1M at the same volume

That is not stated and is not generally true (staff allocation, shared networking, and cluster-level costs do not scale with host count), so the derived rate is presented with more precision than its assumption supports. Recomputed under the stated linear assumption: 155,817 × 32/21 = $237,386 ÷ 5.93×10¹⁰ = $4.00/1M, so the printed $4.01 also does not reproduce exactly.
root_cause: A proportional-scaling assumption was applied silently and the result printed to three significant figures.
correction: State the assumption ("assuming per-host cost scales linearly, which ignores fixed staff and cluster costs") and print $4.00/1M, or drop the figure.
acceptance_test: The $4.01/1M figure is either reproducible from printed inputs or removed.

page_hint: §3 'Scope note on the turn cap'; §4 turn-distribution paragraph; §8 'Measurement results'
quoted_clause: The *recommended operational* policy — deployed in the §8 mini-case and used for fleet sizing in Chapter 17 — caps turns at 3, per the §4 guidance and the 95th-percentile sizing rule (size for the 95th-percentile turn count — §4's illustrative distribution gives p95 T = 3)
observed: The cap is derived from the p95 of a turn distribution that is itself defined under the cap. §8's telemetry is 'the scenario's 30-day telemetry' from a system whose 'maximum of 3 turns' is already in force, so the observed distribution is censored at T = 3 and the '2% exceed the turn limit' class is by construction, not an observation. Using a censored distribution's p95 to set the cap is circular: the rule can only be applied to an uncensored distribution.
evidence: §8: 'The team introduces an agentic layer with a maximum of 3 turns' and 'The scenario's 30-day telemetry shows ... 2% exceed the turn limit and fall back to single-shot'. §4: 'the illustrative turn distribution here has ... 95th percentile T = 3 ... derived from the §8 distribution'. The §8 distribution is therefore the output of the policy that the distribution is used to set.
root_cause: The sizing rule was stated without its measurement precondition; the illustrative distribution was allowed to stand in for the uncensored one.
correction: State the precondition explicitly: 'The 95th-percentile sizing rule requires an *uncensored* turn distribution — measured with the cap disabled, or from a shadow run — because a distribution observed under a cap of 3 is truncated at 3 and its p95 cannot be used to choose the cap. The distribution used here is illustrative and should be read as an uncensored one.'
acceptance_test: Ch 19 states how the turn distribution used for cap selection is obtained, and flags that §8's telemetry is censored by the policy it supports.
